newsitem.title: ITALY: Rome monastery no longer wants Priebke as guest.
newsitem.headline: Rome monastery no longer wants Priebke as guest.

text.p: Italian friars who have been hosting convicted former Nazi officer Erich Priebke at their hillside monastery outside Rome say he is no longer welcome.
"They don't want him any more, he has to leave," Priebke's lawyer Carlo Taormina told Reuters on Tuesday.

Priebke, 84, who last month received a five-year prison sentence from a Rome military court for his role in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, has been living under house arrest at the Franciscan monastery since last year.
Father Andrea Stefani, head of the monastery, said he would let the ex-SS captain stay until a military court decided whether to send him to prison or allow him to be transferred to a private house.

"Priebke himself knows that the time we had established for him to stay here as a guest has expired and he wants to leave as soon as possible so as not to be a burden on the religious life of the convent," he told reporters.
Stefani added that he had originally agreed to keep Priebke only until the trial's conclusion.
The military court should decide where to send Priebke within the next few days, Taormina said.
The lawyer said he had proposed Priebke be transferred to the private Rome residence of Paolo Giachini, who was designated the ex-Nazi officer's legal guardian during the trial.
"Now we're just waiting for the (court) response," said Taormina.
Priebke has about 1-1/2 years of the sentence still to serve, deducting the time he spent in custody after his indictment, according to prosecutor Antonino Intelisano.

Priebke and his co-defendant Karl Hass, 84, were convicted for participating in a 1944 massacre in which SS soldiers rounded up 335 men and boys and shot them in caves outside Rome in retaliation for a partisan attack on German occupying forces.
But it granted some mitigating circumstances and other concessions, reducing the life sentences that both Germans could have faced to five years for Priebke and eight months for Hass.
Hass was then set free because he had already been under house arrest during the hearings.
Priebke was extradited in November 1995 from Argentina where he had lived openly for almost half a century.
On Monday, the military court denied a request to free Priebke from custody despite his conviction.
Taormina had requested on the last day of the trial that Priebke be set free regardless of the verdict, on the basis of his old age and inability to flee. Prosecutors opposed the request.
The lawyer said he would appeal against the decision to the European Commission, the European Union's governing body.
"The ruling is a violation of personal liberty because there is no danger he will flee," he said.
